_comment: Pages = PDF numbering (printed + 8 in the body). Generated by build_index.py; command pages are computed by word search in the extracted text.

book.title: Introduction to Linux: A Hands on Guide
book.author: Machtelt Garrels
book.page_convention: PDF = printed + 8 (printed Introduction 1 = PDF 9; printed Ch. 1 p.7 = PDF 15). PDF 1-8: cover and table of contents. Glossary PDF 212-223.

ajuda-e-documentacao.name: Help and documentation (man, info, apropos, --help)
ajuda-e-documentacao.summary: The book insists on reading the system's own documentation before asking for help: man pages (organized in numbered sections), Info pages, whatis/apropos to discover commands, and the --help option of GNU commands. Shell built-in commands (cd, exit, logout, pwd) have no page of their own.
points: man opens the lowest-numbered section page by default; 'man 5 passwd' chooses the section; 'man -a' shows all (p.33)
apropos searches a name+description index; (1) indicates a user command (p.34)
--help summarizes usage and options of GNU commands (p.34-35)
shell builtins: consult the shell's documentation; MANPATH can hide man pages (p.36)
documentation without a page of its own may be in /usr/share/doc (p.36)
gaps: does not cover tldr, cheat sheets, web search, modern documentation tools
dated: graphical help front ends (Konqueror, gnome-help, nautilus) are period-specific (p.35-36)

sessao-login-root-e-bash.name: Login, root account and Bash shortcuts
sessao-login-root-e-bash.summary: Guidance for the first session: text vs graphical mode, terminal/xterm, prompt, the recommendation to avoid the root account (use it only when needed and log out right after) and the table of Bash shortcuts (Ctrl+A/E/C/D/L/R/Z, Tab, arrows).
points: do not log in as root in graphical mode; root only when the privilege is needed (p.26, 28, 30)
a password typed in text mode shows no echo (p.28)
table 2-1 (initial commands) on p.29; table 2-2 (Bash shortcuts) on p.30
completing names with Tab and Tab Tab (p.30-31)
gaps: does not cover modern session management (systemd-logind), SSH keys at login, MFA
dated: example login screen 'RedHat Linux Release 8.0' (p.28)

filesystem-arvore-e-tipos-de-arquivo.name: Directory tree, file types and directory table
filesystem-arvore-e-tipos-de-arquivo.summary: Everything is a file (or a process). Types: regular, directory, link, special, socket, named pipe, block (table 3-1). Table 3-2 describes the directories below / and the book stresses that names and layout are convention, varying by distribution.
points: 'in UNIX everything is a file; what is not a file is a process' (p.40)
first character of ls -l indicates the type: - d l c s p b (p.41)
table 3-2: /bin /boot /dev /etc /home /lib /lost+found /mnt /opt /proc /root /sbin /tmp /usr /var (p.46)
/tmp is cleared on reboot; do not keep work there (p.46)
'man hier' describes the hierarchy (p.47)
gaps: does not cover the formal FHS, /run, /sys, /srv, /media, /usr merge
dated: layout of a RedHat of the time (p.45-46); /initrd, /misc, /net are period-specific

particoes-swap-e-pontos-de-montagem.name: Partitions, swap, mount points, fstab and df
particoes-swap-e-pontos-de-montagem.summary: Why partition (isolate damage and protect the system from a full disk), partition types (data and swap), the book's rule of swap ≈ 2x RAM, typical partitions (/boot, /usr, /home, /var, /opt), mount points, /etc/fstab and reading df -h.
points: partitioning isolates disasters and keeps a runaway process from filling the whole system (p.42)
journaling protects against power failure, not against bad blocks or logical errors; for that, RAID (p.42)
types 82 (swap) and 83 (data) in fdisk; ext2/ext3 (p.42)
rule: swap with twice the RAM (p.43)
partitions mounted at startup according to /etc/fstab; df -h shows usage and mount points (p.44-45)
gaps: does not cover ext4/XFS/btrfs, LVM, GPT/UEFI, fsck/mkfs, tmpfs, SSD/TRIM, cloud disks
dated: ext2/ext3/ReiserFS/JFS, fdisk and the swap=2xRAM rule are period-specific (p.42-43)

inodes.name: Inodes
inodes.summary: Each file is represented by an inode (owner, type, permissions, times, link count, size, address of the data). The file name is not in the inode: it is in the directory files. Each partition has its own set of inodes and a fixed number of them.
points: inode holds properties and location, but not the name (p.47)
inode numbering is per partition; estimate of 1 inode per 2 to 8 KB (p.47)
ls -i shows inode numbers (p.47)
gaps: does not cover inode exhaustion (df -i), internal FS structures, internal journaling -> os-internals

path-e-variavel-path.name: PATH, absolute/relative paths and which
path-e-variavel-path.summary: The shell looks for the executable in the PATH directories in order and stops at the first one found; this explains 'command not found' and cases where a user's program hides another with the same name. which -a shows all occurrences; export PATH=... changes only the current session.
points: search stops at the first hit, even without walking the whole PATH (p.48)
example of a homemade wc in ~/bin that shadows /usr/bin/wc (p.48-49)
export is valid only for the session; to persist, shell configuration files (p.49)
a path that starts with / is absolute; otherwise it is relative; ./ runs from the current directory (p.49)
which diagnoses 'command not found' and shows aliases (p.62)
gaps: does not cover hash/rehash in detail, command -v, type, safe PATH in scripts/cron/sudo

shells-e-etc-shells.name: Shell types (sh, bash, csh, tcsh, ksh)
shells-e-etc-shells.summary: Definitions of shell such as 'language for talking to the computer'. bash is a superset of sh (what runs in sh runs in bash, not the reverse); /bin/sh is usually a link to bash in compatibility mode; the user's default shell is in /etc/passwd and the list in /etc/shells. Appendix C compares common and different features among sh, bash, ksh and csh.
points: bash is compatible with sh, but not the reverse (p.50)
/bin/sh is usually a link to Bash in compatibility mode (p.51)
default shell in /etc/passwd; echo $SHELL shows the shell in use (p.51)
Appendix C: table C-1 common features (p.208-209) and C-2 distinct features (p.209-211)
gaps: does not cover zsh, dash, fish, POSIX sh in depth
dated: csh/tcsh/ksh are treated as period-specific; zsh absent

home-quota-e-limpeza.name: Home directory, quota and organization
home-quota-e-limpeza.summary: Home is the default destination at login (HOME, ~). The book suggests organization (personal bin, private directories with chmod 700) and ways to free space: truncating with '> file', tail to keep only the end, log handling, .forward, symlinks instead of copies, ulimit and the z* tools for compressed files.
points: quota -v shows limits; without quota, no limitation (p.51, 119)
'> file' truncates to 0 bytes; touch creates empty/updates the date (p.120)
tail -5 to keep only the last items (p.120)
symbolic link to /dev/null on logs: only if the program does not recreate the file (p.120)
ulimit -a shows limits; core dumps (p.121-122)
gaps: does not cover logrotate in detail, cgroups, modern FS quotas

listar-e-identificar-arquivos.name: ls, colors/suffixes and file
listar-e-identificar-arquivos.summary: ls with options (-a for hidden, -l long, -t/-r by date, -d, -F/--color). Tables of colors and suffixes. file guesses the format (it can be fooled) and helps avoid opening binaries with text tools.
points: files that start with a dot are hidden; . and .. exist in every directory (p.56)
ls -latr leaves the most recent at the end (p.56)
file is only a guess; it can be fooled (p.58)
gaps: does not cover stat, tree, lsattr in detail

criar-copiar-mover-remover.name: mkdir, mv, cp, rm and rmdir
criar-copiar-mover-remover.summary: Basic file operations. There is no trash can in the shell: removal is final; -i on rm/cp/mv asks for confirmation. mkdir -p creates trees; cp -R copies recursively; mv renames and moves.
points: mkdir -p creates intermediate directories (p.60)
Linux is case-sensitive; there are not two files with the same name in the same directory (p.60)
no trash can in the shell: what was removed only comes back from backup (p.61)
-i for rm, cp and mv (p.61)
gaps: does not cover trash-cli, snapshots, rm -rf in depth

busca-glob-find-locate-grep.name: Globbing, find, locate and grep
busca-glob-find-locate-grep.summary: The shell expands * ? [ ] before the command. find walks the tree by name/size/date and runs actions; -exec calls the command once per file, whereas find | xargs is more economical. locate uses a daily index (fast, may be stale) and slocate respects permissions. grep filters lines; Ctrl+R searches the history; special characters require escaping with a backslash.
points: find <path> -name <pattern> searches by name, not by content (p.62)
test the selection before triggering -exec rm; xargs reduces calls (p.63)
locate is based on an index updated once a day (p.63)
grep -a/-i; Ctrl+R does reverse search in the history (p.64-65)
escape: less \* ; cat This\ File (p.65)
gaps: does not cover find -print0/xargs -0, fd, ripgrep, extended regex in depth
dated: slocate and locate's '1999' date are period-specific (p.63)

visualizar-conteudo-less-head-tail.name: cat, less/more, head and tail
visualizar-conteudo-less-head-tail.summary: cat dumps the file; more/less page (less is the GNU version with search and backward scrolling); head/tail show the start/end; tail -f follows growing files, used by administrators on logs.
points: less is the pager used by man (p.66)
tail -f follows logs (p.66)
check the type with file before opening (p.65)
gaps: does not cover journalctl, multitail, bat

links-hard-e-simbolicos.name: Hard and symbolic links (ln)
links-hard-e-simbolicos.summary: A hard link associates several names with the same inode and does not cross partitions; a symbolic link is a small file with the target's path, crosses partitions and breaks if the target disappears. A hard link and the original file have the same size; symlinks are small.
points: hard links share an inode and do not cross partitions (p.66-67)
symlinks hold the target's path; removing the target makes the link useless (p.67)
ln -s target name (p.68)
gaps: does not cover link counts on directories, bind mounts, reflink

permissoes-chmod-umask-chown.name: Permissions: rwx, chmod, umask, chown/chgrp, groups
permissoes-chmod-umask-chown.summary: Each file has an owner, a group and 'others', with read/write/execute (r=4, w=2, x=1). chmod accepts symbolic form (u+x, u+rwx,go-rwx) or numeric; table 3-9 lists common combinations. umask is subtracted from 777 (directories) or 666 (files); chown/chgrp change ownership (restricted to root). id shows uid/gid; newgrp switches the active group.
points: three categories u/g/o and rwx order (p.68-69); codes 4/2/1 (p.69)
'bad interpreter: Permission denied' on a script without x: chmod u+x (p.70)
fewer than 3 digits: leading zeros; fourth digit = special modes (p.71)
user private group scheme; newgrp and gpasswd (p.71)
umask 0002 -> files 664, directories 775; root usually has 022 (p.72-73)
chown user: file; chgrp; -R recursive; restricted for unprivileged users (p.73-74)
gaps: does not cover ACLs (setfacl), SELinux/AppArmor, capabilities, chmod X, chattr/lsattr in detail

modos-especiais-suid-sgid-sticky.name: SUID, SGID and sticky bit
modos-especiais-suid-sgid-sticky.summary: Special modes allow tasks that ordinary permissions would prevent. SUID/SGID make the executable run with the file's owner/group (examples: passwd, write/wall); SGID on a directory inherits the group; sticky on a directory (/var/tmp) prevents deleting others' files. The book asks for minimal use, because of the security risk.
points: sticky bit: letter t; chmod o+t directory (p.74)
SUID/SGID: letter s; the process runs with the file's permissions (p.74, 86-87)
SGID on a directory: new files inherit the group; moved files keep their original owner/group (p.74)
use special modes as little as possible, since they carry risks (p.86)
gaps: does not cover SUID auditing (find -perm), nosuid in mount, capabilities
dated: use of sticky on executable files (in-memory cache) is historical (p.74)

processos-tipos-e-atributos.name: Processes: types, attributes, ps/top/pstree, fork/exec, zombie
processos-tipos-e-atributos.summary: Interactive processes (foreground/background), automatic (at/batch) and daemons. Attributes: PID, PPID, nice, TTY, real and effective UID/GID. ps is a snapshot, top updates periodically, pstree shows relationships. Processes are born by fork+exec; init is PID 1; a zombie is a terminated child not reaped by its parent; termination returns an exit status.
points: process types (p.79-81); attributes (p.81)
ps -ef | grep user; pgrep avoids listing grep itself (p.82)
login shell appears with a hyphen in the list (p.82)
top and uptime; data in /proc (p.82-83)
fork and exec; init is the first process; zombie (p.84-85)
exit status: 0 = success (true); codes specific to each program (p.85)
gaps: does not cover scheduling, virtual memory, concurrency, internal threads -> os-internals (OSTEP)
dated: examples with mozilla/gnome (p.81-83); the claim that grep returns -1 with no matches is imprecise (in practice, 1) (p.85)

jobs-sinais-e-kill.name: Job control, signals and kill
jobs-sinais-e-kill.summary: Job control: & for background, Ctrl+Z suspends, bg/fg, jobs, %n. Signals: SIGTERM(15) ends in an orderly way, SIGINT(2) can be ignored, SIGKILL(9) cannot, SIGHUP(1) makes daemons reread their configuration. Recommendation: try -15 first, only then -9 and confirm with ps|grep.
points: table 4-1 of process control (p.80); screen keeps sessions (p.80)
table 4-2: SIGTERM 15, SIGINT 2, SIGKILL 9, SIGHUP 1 (p.86)
try SIGTERM first; SIGKILL as a last resort; check with ps | grep PID (p.98)
xkill sends SIGKILL: only for hung applications (p.99)
gaps: does not cover nohup/disown, pkill/killall, SIGSTOP/SIGCONT, tmux, systemd units

boot-init-e-runlevels.name: Boot, GRUB, SysV init, runlevels and shutdown
boot-init-e-runlevels.summary: Boot sequence (BIOS, MBR, GRUB/LILO, kernel, init). init reads /etc/inittab, sets the default runlevel and runs K (stop) and S (start) scripts via links in rcN.d that point to /etc/init.d. Runlevels: 0, 1/S, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Tools chkconfig/update-rc.d/ntsysv. shutdown -h/-r.
points: GRUB reads the configuration at every boot (p.89)
init reads /etc/inittab, runs K scripts with stop and S with start (p.89)
links in /etc/rcN.d point to /etc/init.d; order by the numbers in the name (p.90)
runlevels of the example inittab: 0 halt, 1 single, 2, 3, 4 unused, 5 X11, 6 reboot (p.91)
single-user mode to fix a corrupted inittab/passwd (p.91)
shutdown -h / -r; reboot and halt (p.92)
gaps: does not cover systemd (units, targets, journalctl), UEFI, initramfs, GRUB2, Upstart, OpenRC in detail
dated: this ENTIRE topic is [DATED]: SysV init, runlevels, lilo, BIOS/MBR, ntsysv/yast/DrakConf

desempenho-carga-nice-e-recursos.name: Performance: time, load, nice/renice, CPU, memory, I/O
desempenho-carga-nice-e-recursos.summary: time measures duration (real/user/sys); normal load depends on the system (track it to know your normal). high nice = nicer process; renice changes a running process; do not use it on interactive ones. For CPU: run heavy jobs off-peak, stop what is unnecessary. Memory: paging/swap makes everything slow. I/O: few tools at the time; typical bottlenecks are network and disk.
points: Bash's built-in time vs /usr/bin/time (p.93-94)
a load of 0 or of 67 can be normal depending on the machine; measure regularly (p.94)
high nice = less important; do not 'nice' interactive processes (p.95)
paging/swap: the system does not crash, but becomes much slower (p.95)
ps, vmstat, top and iostat give clues about I/O (p.96)
gaps: does not cover perf, strace, sar, cgroups, PSI, modern observability -> other agents
dated: renice 20 as '1/5 of the CPU' (p.98) is imprecise; the modern range is -20..19

agendamento-sleep-at-cron.name: Scheduling: sleep, at, batch, cron and crontab
agendamento-sleep-at-cron.summary: Three forms of deferred execution: sleep (wait), at (set time, once; atq/atrm; avoid round hours) and cron (periodic). batch runs when the load allows (< 0.8). crontab has 5 time fields (min, hour, day of month, month, day of week 0-7), SHELL/PATH/MAILTO variables and, in /etc/crontab, the user column. crontab -e edits safely; the job's output goes by e-mail to the owner.
points: three types of deferred execution (p.99)
at: -m sends mail; atq/atrm; avoid round hours (p.100)
cron reads /var/spool/cron, /etc/cron.d, /etc/crontab every minute; runs as the crontab's owner (p.100)
fields and lists/ranges; Sunday = 0 or 7 (p.101)
crontab -e; no need to restart cron; output by e-mail in /var/spool/mail (p.101-102)
gaps: does not cover systemd timers, cronie/fcron in detail, flock, @reboot, / (steps) and day/month names
dated: examples with dates from 2001-2003; anacron only mentioned (glossary)

redirecionamento-pipes-e-filtros.name: Redirection (>, >>, <, 2>&1), pipes, tee, filters
redirecionamento-pipes-e-filtros.summary: stdin(0), stdout(1), stderr(2). '>' creates or overwrites (careful), '>>' appends, '<' feeds input, '|' chains. 'cmd > f 2>&1' sends both to f; 'cmd 2>&1 > f' only stdout. No space between the number and '>'. tee writes and displays. noclobber protects against overwriting. Filters: grep (-v, -i, -r), sort, uniq.
points: '>' overwrites or creates; set -o noclobber protects (p.105-106)
'> file' alone truncates (p.106)
'<' for input; '>>' appends (p.106-107)
descriptors 0/1/2; the order of '2>&1' matters; '2 > file' with a space gives an error (p.108)
make all 2>&1 | less; tee and tee -a (p.109)
sort -nk 5; sort | uniq or sort -u (p.110-111)
gaps: does not cover process substitution, here-strings, exec with descriptors, named pipes (mkfifo), sed/awk in depth

editores-vi-emacs.name: Text editors (vi/vim and Emacs)
editores-vi-emacs.summary: The book advocates mastering at least one terminal text editor. Vim has two modes (command and insert); it lists basic commands (dd, dw, x, :w, :q, :q!, :wq, /search, :s///g, yy, p, :recover) and recommends vimtutor.
points: vi works on practically every UNIX (p.114)
two modes; Esc returns to command mode (p.114-116)
basic commands on p.115
do not edit configuration files with an office suite (p.117)
gaps: does not cover nano, VS Code, ed/ex, advanced vim configuration
dated: gedit/kedit/xedit (p.117)

variaveis-de-ambiente-e-export.name: Environment variables, export and MANPATH
variaveis-de-ambiente-e-export.summary: Environment variables are inherited by child processes (a copy); ordinary shell variables are not. Assigning without export does not reach other programs. export VAR=value does both. Table 7-1 lists standard variables (PATH, HOME, PS1, LANG, EDITOR...).
points: the environment is copied to children; shell vars are not (p.122)
assigning without export does not propagate; export VARIABLE=value (p.123)
table 7-1 (p.124)
printenv lists variables (p.122)
gaps: does not cover env -i, declare -x, readonly, variables in systemd/cron/sudo

arquivos-de-inicializacao-do-shell.name: Bash startup files (profile, bashrc, logout)
arquivos-de-inicializacao-do-shell.summary: A login shell reads /etc/profile and then the first existing one among ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile; ~/.bashrc is the personal counterpart of /etc/bashrc; .bash_logout runs on exit. source applies changes to the current shell.
points: login shell read order (p.124)
example of /etc/profile, profile.d, .bash_profile, .bash_login, /etc/bashrc, .bash_logout (p.125-127)
source ~/.bashrc applies changes to the current environment (p.126)
default umask set in these files (p.127)
gaps: does not cover login/non-login differences in modern detail, ~/.profile on Debian/Ubuntu, zsh rc
dated: the content of /etc/profile and /etc/bashrc is from a RedHat of the time

prompt-ps1.name: Bash prompt (PS1)
prompt-ps1.summary: The prompt is the PS1 variable; the book shows how to save the original prompt, test changes on the command line and fix them in ~/.bashrc, with escape sequences such as \u, \h, \w, \t and colors.
points: save PS1 in another variable before testing (p.128)
PS1 examples (p.128-129)
persist in ~/.bashrc (p.129)
gaps: does not cover PROMPT_COMMAND in depth, git prompts, starship

shell-scripts-basicos.name: Shell scripts (the little the book covers)
shell-scripts-basicos.summary: A script is a text file with commands; it becomes executable with chmod; the #! line chooses the interpreter (#!/bin/bash guarantees Bash). The book shows scripts of 1 to 15 lines (hello, who|cut|sort, .old copy with for, init script with case/start/stop) and suggests echo for debugging. It points to a Bash course and to Advanced Bash Scripting for going deeper.
points: script = text file; running 'script ARGS' is equivalent to 'bash script ARGS' (p.129)
#!: the rest of the line indicates the interpreter; #!/bin/bash guarantees Bash (p.129)
examples: hello.sh, who|cut|sort -u, makebackupfiles.sh with for and LIST=`ls` (p.130)
echo after doubtful steps helps find the error (p.130)
init script with case/$1, usage and exit 1/exit 0; uses sh for portability (p.130-131)
exercise: the copy script generates errors with directories; use find (p.143)
gaps: does NOT cover: if/while/functions in detail, set -e/-u/-o pipefail, trap in scripts, getopts, advanced quoting, here-doc, arrays, shellcheck, portability best practices
dated: the scripts use backticks and RedHat init scripts (p.130-131)

x-window-e-ambiente-grafico.name: X Window, display, managers and xorg.conf
x-window-e-ambiente-grafico.summary: X is a network-transparent window system: the X server controls the screen and the clients are the programs. DISPLAY has the form host:display.screen. Window and desktop managers are clients. Configuration in xorg.conf/XF86Config (back up before editing). Remote display via xhost+DISPLAY or via SSH.
points: X clients and server; display name (p.132-133)
window manager vs desktop manager (p.133)
xorg.conf and XF86Config; back up before touching (p.133-134)
server vs client and remote (p.185-186)
gaps: does not cover Wayland, compositors, modern VNC, systemd graphical.target
dated: the ENTIRE topic is period-specific: XFree86/XF86Config, old Gnome/KDE

configuracoes-regionais.name: Keyboard, fonts, date/time (NTP), language and encoding
configuracoes-regionais.summary: loadkeys for the console keyboard, ntpd/ntpdate for time, tzconfig for time zone, LANG/LANGUAGE for language and recode to convert encodings; the book notes that the default became en_US.UTF-8 and that problems appear with systems lacking UTF-8 support.
points: loadkeys and XkbLayout (p.134)
ntpd/ntpdate; do not run ntpdate with ntpd active (p.135)
LANG, UTF-8, recode (p.135)
gaps: does not cover timedatectl, chrony, localectl
dated: tzconfig/ntpdate/loadkeys as presented are period-specific

pacotes-rpm-deb-apt.name: Packages: RPM, DEB, APT, yum and kernel
pacotes-rpm-deb-apt.summary: RPM and DEB formats, source code (tarball + README + gcc) and the APT, yum, up2date, YaST, urpmi managers. The book advocates updating right after installing and regularly, installing a new kernel alongside the old one (rpm -i, grub.conf with two entries) and mounting/ejecting CDs correctly.
points: rpm -Uvh, -qa, -qf, -e; kernel with -i (p.137)
dpkg -l, -S (p.138)
source: README and gcc (p.138)
apt-get update/upgrade/install; su - -c (p.139-140)
new kernel coexisting with the old one in grub.conf (p.140-141)
mount/umount/eject of CD; device busy -> lsof (p.141-142)
gaps: does not cover dnf, zypper, snap/flatpak, pacman, modern signatures, containers
dated: this ENTIRE topic is [DATED]: up2date, urpmi, dselect, Red Carpet, old yum

backup-tar-gzip-rsync.name: Backup: tar, gzip/bzip2, dd, rsync, media
backup-tar-gzip-rsync.summary: Prepare the data with tar (archive directories, not loose files), compress with gzip/bzip2, and send to media or another host. tar -N (by date) and -g (snapshot file) make incrementals; -g is better than -N. rsync copies to a local directory, USB or remote. Also: dd, fdformat/mformat, mkisofs+cdrecord, dump/restore.
points: tar: -c -x -t -v -f -j; use GNU tar (p.152-153)
archiving a directory avoids scattering files on extraction (p.153)
incremental with -N (by date) and its limitation; -g with a snapshot file (p.154-155)
gzip removes the original; tar zxvf / jxvf (p.155)
rsync -avz source/ destination (p.160)
dd and dump/restore copy bit by bit (p.157, 160)
gaps: does not cover restic/borg/duplicity, LVM/ZFS snapshots, 3-2-1, formal restore testing, retention, RPO/RTO
dated: floppy, CD-R, tapes, jazz drive, mkbootdisk, HAL (p.156-159)

criptografia-gpg.name: Encryption with GnuPG
criptografia-gpg.summary: GnuPG generates a key pair (private protected by a passphrase, public for correspondents); gpg -e -r encrypts for a recipient, gpg -d -o decrypts. Without the password, the data is lost; not even the administrator can recover it.
points: key pair; private with passphrase (p.161)
gpg -e -r and gpg -d -o (p.162-163)
no password, no data (p.163)
gaps: does not cover current gpg2/gpg-agent, age, disk encryption (LUKS), key management/KMS
dated: sizes and algorithms in the example (DSA 1024/ElGamal) are period-specific

rede-modelo-protocolos-e-config.name: Networking: layered model, protocols, configuration files
rede-modelo-protocolos-e-config.summary: Simplified OSI model in 4 layers (application, transport, network, network access). Overview of TCP/IP, IPv6, PPP/PPPoE, ISDN, AppleTalk and SMB/Samba. Common network files: /etc/hosts (never remove localhost), /etc/resolv.conf (search/nameserver) and /etc/nsswitch.conf (order 'files dns').

/etc/hosts, resolv.conf and nsswitch.conf (p.169)
information needed to configure the network (p.168)

rede-comandos-ip-ifconfig-netstat.name: Network commands: ip, ifconfig, netstat, host, ping, traceroute, whois
rede-comandos-ip-ifconfig-netstat.summary: ip (and ifconfig/route on old systems) shows and configures interfaces and routes. Typical interfaces: lo (do not touch), eth0, wlan0, ppp0. netstat -nr shows routes (0.0.0.0 = default gateway). host/dig query DNS, ping tests reachability, traceroute/tracepath shows the path, whois queries domains.

servicos-de-rede-inetd-mail-web-ftp-dns.name: Network services: standalone vs (x)inetd, mail, web, proxy, FTP, DNS, DHCP, PAM, LDAP
servicos-de-rede-inetd-mail-web-ftp-dns.summary: Services can run on their own (standalone) or under the (x)inetd super-server, which starts the daemon on demand. Overview of mail servers, IMAP vs POP, Apache, proxies (http_proxy), FTP (insecure; use sftp), DNS/BIND, DHCP, local authentication (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow), PAM (/etc/pam.d, 4 elements) and LDAP.

acesso-remoto-ssh-telnet-x-vnc.name: Remote access: telnet/rsh vs SSH, scp/sftp, keys, X forwarding, VNC
acesso-remoto-ssh-telnet-x-vnc.summary: rsh/rlogin/telnet are insecure; use SSH. The book shows telnet only for testing servers (SMTP port 25, HTTP port 80). SSH encrypts everything, verifies the host's identity (known_hosts; warns if the key changes), forwards X11 and ports; scp/sftp replace rcp/ftp; ssh-keygen creates keys with a passphrase (not recoverable).

seguranca-de-rede-e-intrusao.name: Network security, firewall, IDS and break-in recovery
seguranca-de-rede-e-intrusao.summary: Principles: run the minimum of services (check with netstat -l), update regularly, firewall with rules (Netfilter/iptables packet filter, TCP wrappers, proxies), log only the abnormal, IDS (tripwire for host, Snort for network), avoid root login (prefer sudo), SSH/SSL instead of telnet/FTP. Checklist of break-in signs and recovery order: disconnect, investigate, back up data, reinstall, new passwords, restore, update, re-examine, reconnect.
points: few services; netstat -l | grep tcp; 'things to avoid' list (p.191-192)
update right away and always (p.192)
firewall, packet filter, stateful inspection, TCP wrappers, proxies (p.192-193)

break-in signs (p.194); recovery order (p.194-195)

apendices-dos-vs-linux-e-recursos-do-she.name: Appendix B (DOS vs Linux) and Appendix C (shell features)
apendices-dos-vs-linux-e-recursos-do-she.summary: Appendix B translates DOS commands to Linux (cls=clear, copy=cp, del=rm, dir=ls, move/ren=mv, find=grep...).
